lessons.title: Cargo: Build Then Run
lessons.objective: Create, build and run a Rust project with Cargo, and explain how compiling differs from running a Python script.
lessons.hook: In Rust, many bugs are caught before the program ever runs, because compiling is a separate step.
lessons.aside: rustup installs and updates the Rust toolchain, much as pyenv manages Python versions.
lessons.explain: Python runs your source file directly. Rust compiles it first into a standalone binary. Cargo is Rust's build tool and package manager, similar to pip and venv combined. The command `cargo new hello` creates Cargo.toml and src/main.rs. Cargo.toml lists dependencies, similar to pyproject.toml. `cargo build` compiles the project into target/debug/. `cargo run` builds the project and then runs it. If the compiler finds an error, no binary is produced and nothing runs. Example: `cargo new hello && cd hello && cargo run` prints Hello, world!

lessons.title: Immutable by Default
lessons.objective: Declare variables with let, make them mutable with mut, and use shadowing.
lessons.hook: Python lets any name change at any time; Rust makes you say so up front, which prevents a whole class of bugs.
lessons.explain: In Rust, `let x = 5;` creates an immutable variable. Writing `x = 6;` afterwards is a compile error. To allow changes, write `let mut x = 5;`, and then `x = 6;` works. Shadowing is different: `let x = x + 1;` declares a new variable that reuses the name. The old one becomes hidden; it is not mutated. Shadowing can even change the type. Example: `let s = "42"; let s: i32 = s.parse().unwrap();` turns a text value into a number under the same name.

Shadowing can change the type
angles: `let` is like a constant label, and `mut` is permission to edit it. A second `let` with the same name throws the old label away and makes a fresh one.
Imagine a Python where every variable is final unless you mark it. Rust is that language, and `mut` is the mark.
claims: Rust variables are immutable by default
let mut allows reassignment
Shadowing creates a new binding and can change type

lessons.title: Static Types and Inference
lessons.objective: Read and write type annotations, know the default numeric types, and convert between numeric types explicitly.
lessons.hook: Python type hints are optional suggestions; Rust types are enforced, and that is where much of Rust's safety comes from.
lessons.explain: Every Rust value has a type that is known at compile time. You often don't have to write it, because the compiler infers it: `let n = 5;` gets the type i32, which is the default integer type. `let f = 2.0;` gets f64, the default float type. You can annotate a type yourself: `let big: i64 = 5;`. Rust never converts between numeric types implicitly. `let total: i64 = n + big;` is a compile error when n is an i32. You must write `n as i64 + big`. Unlike Python hints, mypy-style warnings are not optional here: a type mismatch stops compilation.

The compiler infers types when you omit them
The default integer type is i32
The default float type is f64
Rust never converts numeric types implicitly; use `as`

lessons.title: Functions and Expressions
lessons.objective: Write functions with typed parameters and return types, and return values using a final expression.
lessons.hook: A single semicolon decides whether a Rust function returns your value, so it's worth learning early.
lessons.explain: Functions use `fn`. Every parameter must have a type, and the return type follows `->`. Example: `fn double(n: i32) -> i32 { n * 2 }`. The last expression in the body, written without a semicolon, is the return value. Adding a semicolon (`n * 2;`) turns it into a statement that produces (), the unit type. The function then fails to compile, because it promised to return an i32. `return` exists too, but it is mostly used for early exits. Blocks and `if` are also expressions: `let s = if n > 0 { "pos" } else { "neg" };`.

The return type is written after `->`
The last expression without a semicolon is the return value

`if` is an expression that can produce a value
angles: Read the last line of a block, without its semicolon, as an implicit `return`. The semicolon means throw the value away.

lessons.title: String vs &str
lessons.objective: Tell owned String from borrowed &str and choose the right one.
lessons.hook: Python has one string type and Rust has two; mixing them up causes most beginner type errors.
lessons.explain: `String` is an owned, growable string stored on the heap. You can push text onto it: `let mut s = String::from("hi"); s.push_str("!");`. `&str` is a string slice, a borrowed view into string data that someone else owns. String literals such as `"hi"` have the type `&'static str`, meaning they live for the whole program. You can borrow a &str from a String with `&s` or `s.as_str()`. Rust has two types because of ownership: String owns its data, and &str only looks at it.

angles: String is a notebook you own and can write in. &str is a photo of some pages: you can read it, but you can't add to it.

lessons.title: The Ownership Rules
lessons.objective: State the three ownership rules and predict when a value is dropped.
lessons.hook: Rust has no garbage collector; ownership is how it frees memory safely.
lessons.aside: Drop is like Python's __del__ being called at a guaranteed point, at the end of scope, rather than whenever the reference count happens to reach zero.
lessons.explain: Python frees objects through reference counting and a garbage collector. Rust uses three ownership rules instead, and they are checked at compile time. First, each value has an owner, which is a variable. Second, there is only one owner at a time. Third, when the owner goes out of scope, the value is dropped and its memory is freed. Example: `{ let s = String::from("hi"); }` creates s inside the block. At the closing brace, s goes out of scope and the String's heap memory is freed automatically. There is no runtime collector, and you never call free yourself.
key_facts: Each value has an owner
There is only one owner at a time
When the owner goes out of scope, the value is dropped
Rust has no garbage collector; ownership is checked at compile time

lessons.title: Moves, Copies and Clone
lessons.objective: Predict whether assignment moves or copies a value, and use clone when you need two independent values.
lessons.hook: `b = a` in Python shares one object; in Rust it usually transfers ownership, and this is the first thing that surprises Python developers.
lessons.explain: In Python, `b = a` makes both names refer to the same object. In Rust, `let b = a;` with a String moves ownership to b. After that, using a is a compile error, because a value can have only one owner. Passing a value to a function moves it in the same way. Simple types such as i32, f64, bool and char implement Copy, so assigning them copies the value and both variables stay usable. To get two independent Strings, call `a.clone()`, which makes a deep copy. Example: `let a = String::from("hi"); let b = a; println!("{a}");` fails with an error about borrowing a moved value.

Using a moved-from variable is a compile error
Passing a value to a function moves it
i32, f64, bool and char are Copy, so assignment copies them
`.clone()` makes a deep copy

lessons.title: Borrowing with &
lessons.objective: Pass values to functions by shared reference so the caller keeps ownership.
lessons.hook: Borrowing lets functions use your data without taking it, which is how most Rust functions are written.
lessons.explain: A reference, `&T`, lets you use a value without taking ownership of it. This is called borrowing. Example: `fn len(s: &String) -> usize { s.len() }`, called as `len(&name)`, leaves name owned by the caller and usable afterwards. You can have any number of shared references at the same time. Shared references are read-only, so trying to modify through `&T` is a compile error. A reference must never outlive the value it points to. The compiler rejects code where the owner would be dropped while a borrow is still in use.

After passing `&name`, the caller can still use name

lessons.title: &mut and the Borrow Checker
lessons.objective: Use mutable references and fix the borrow checker's errors about mixing & and &mut.
lessons.hook: The borrow checker's main rule rules out data races and many cases of changing data while it is being read, before the code runs.
lessons.explain: `&mut T` is a mutable reference. It lets a function change a value it doesn't own: `fn bump(n: &mut i32) { *n += 1; }`, called as `bump(&mut x)`. The variable x must be declared mut. The rule is that at any moment you may have either one &mut or any number of & references to a value, but not both. The borrow checker enforces this rule at compile time. A borrow lasts until its last use, not until the end of the scope. Example: `let r = &v; v.push(1); println!("{r:?}");` fails, because r is still used after the push. If you move the println above the push, it compiles.

You can only take `&mut x` if x is declared mut
At any time you may have either one &mut or any number of &, not both

lessons.title: Option Instead of None
lessons.objective: Represent missing values with Option and handle both cases with match.
lessons.hook: Many Python crashes are AttributeErrors on None; Rust makes that kind of mistake a compile error.
lessons.explain: Rust has no null value. A value that might be missing has the type `Option<T>`, which is either `Some(value)` or `None`. Example: `v.get(10)` on a vector returns `Option<&i32>`, not a value that might be null. You cannot use an Option<T> as if it were a T, because the types differ and the compiler stops you. Use `match` to handle both cases: `match v.get(10) { Some(x) => println!("{x}"), None => println!("missing") }`. match must cover every case, so forgetting the None arm is a compile error. `.unwrap()` extracts the value but panics if it is None.
key_facts: Rust has no null
`Option<T>` is either `Some(value)` or `None`
You cannot use an Option<T> as a T directly
`match` must cover every case
`.unwrap()` panics on None

predict.q: `let v = vec![1]; let x: i32 = v.get(0);` What happens?
options: Compile error: expected i32, found Option

angles: Option is a labeled box. Some means something is inside, and None means it's empty. You have to open the box before you can use what's inside.
It works like Python's Optional[int] hint, except the compiler forces you to check for None before you use the value.
